spec.query: SELECT mean("value") FROM "amd_uncore" WHERE ("host" =~ /^$host$/ AND "scope" = 'system' AND ("metric" = 'Total_Mem_RdBw_GB_s' OR "metric" = 'Total_Mem_WrBw_GB_s')) AND $timeFilter GROUP BY time($__interval), "metric" fill(previous)

spec.description:
System-wide memory bandwidth split by direction. `Total_Mem_RdBw_GB_s` = reads, `Total_Mem_WrBw_GB_s` = writes. Ratio typically 5:1 to 20:1 read:write on trading hosts because reads dominate strategy computation.

Sudden write spikes may indicate log rotation, cache flushes, journalctl compaction, or memory pressure triggering paging. Investigate with `iostat -x 1` on the host.

Sustained write bandwidth above 2 GB/s system-wide is unusual for HFT — check for processes doing heavy disk I/O or unexpected memory churn.
spec.title: Memory Read vs Write Bandwidth — System (GB/s)

spec.query: SELECT mean("value") FROM "amd_uncore" WHERE ("host" =~ /^$host$/ AND "scope" = 'package-0' AND "metric" =~ /^Mem_Ch_[A-L]_RdBw_GB_s$/) AND $timeFilter GROUP BY time($__interval), "metric" fill(previous)

spec.description:
Read bandwidth per memory channel on package 0. Each socket has 12 DDR5 channels labeled A-L. Uniform bar heights = balanced allocation across channels (good NUMA behavior).

Sudden asymmetry (one channel very hot, others quiet) indicates memory allocated on a single NUMA node while cores access it from many places. Not fatal but suboptimal — throughput becomes single-channel limited.

For NUMA-balanced allocation, ensure trading processes use `numactl --interleave=all` or bind to the socket where their data lives. To see current mapping: `cat /proc/<pid>/numa_maps`.
spec.title: Memory Channel Read Bandwidth — Package-0 (GB/s per channel A-L)

spec.query: SELECT mean("value") FROM "amd_uncore" WHERE ("host" =~ /^$host$/ AND "scope" = 'package-1' AND "metric" =~ /^Mem_Ch_[A-L]_RdBw_GB_s$/) AND $timeFilter GROUP BY time($__interval), "metric" fill(previous)

spec.description:
Read bandwidth per memory channel on package 1 (second socket). Same 12-channel layout as package-0.

Compare against the package-0 panel — under a uniformly distributed workload, both packages should look similar in shape and magnitude. Systematic asymmetry across packages suggests workload placement issues rather than channel-level imbalance.

On single-socket hosts (48-core, 96-core SKUs), this panel will be empty.
spec.title: Memory Channel Read Bandwidth — Package-1 (GB/s per channel A-L)

spec.query: SELECT mean("value") FROM "amd_uncore" WHERE ("host" =~ /^$host$/ AND "scope" = 'system' AND ("metric" = 'xGMI_Outbound_Data_Bytes_GB_s' OR "metric" = 'Local_Inbound_Read_Data_Bytes_GB_s' OR "metric" = 'Remote_Inbound_Read_Data_Bytes_GB_s')) AND $timeFilter GROUP BY time($__interval), "metric" fill(previous)

spec.description:
Cross-socket data traffic over AMD Infinity Fabric xGMI links. Three series:

• `xGMI outbound` — data leaving this socket for the other socket.
• `Local Inbound Read` — reads served from this socket's own memory (good NUMA locality).
• `Remote Inbound Read` — reads coming from the other socket's memory (poor NUMA locality; bad).

Good NUMA behavior: Local Inbound greatly exceeds Remote Inbound; xGMI stays low. If Remote Inbound spikes, threads on this socket are reading memory pinned to the other socket — check `numactl --show` for the trading process, verify memory allocation matches CPU affinity.
spec.title: Data Fabric — xGMI + Inbound Reads (GB/s)

spec.query: SELECT non_negative_derivative(mean("value"), 1s) FROM "amd_core" WHERE ("host" =~ /^$host$/ AND "event" = 'ex_ret_instr' AND "role" = 'trading') AND $timeFilter GROUP BY time($__interval), "core" fill(null)

spec.description:
Rate of retired (successfully completed) instructions per trading core. Retired means the CPU did useful work — speculative work that got squashed is not counted. Source: perf event `ex_ret_instr` from `amd_core`.

HFT hot loops typically 1-3 billion instr/sec per active core. Idle cores stay near 0 — this is expected. All trading cores near 0 for >5 minutes suggests the workload has died.

For actual IPC (instructions per cycle), see the dedicated "Computed ratios" section — v3 ships pre-computed IPC values that avoid Grafana math node fragility. To identify what's on a specific core, run `sudo pmu-core-explain <core>` on the host.
spec.title: Retired Instructions Rate — Per Trading Core (instr/sec)

spec.query: SELECT non_negative_derivative(mean("value"), 1s) FROM "amd_l3" WHERE ("host" =~ /^$host$/ AND "event" = 'l3_lookup_state.l3_miss') AND $timeFilter GROUP BY time($__interval), "ccx" fill(null)

spec.description:
Rate of L3 cache misses per CCX (each CCX is a group of 8 cores sharing one L3 slice on Zen 5/5c). High miss rate = memory-bound workload, working set doesn't fit in the 32 MiB per CCX. Source: `l3_lookup_state.l3_miss` from `amd_l3`.

Normal quiet CCXs sit below 100K/sec. CCXs hosting network-ingest threads can reach 20-30M/sec because packet data can't be cached. Sudden spikes on previously-quiet CCXs indicate workload shift.

To identify what's driving misses on a CCX, run `sudo pmu-core-explain <cpu>` on any core in that CCX (cores 0-7 = ccx 0, 8-15 = ccx 1, etc.). See also the dedicated L3 hit ratio panel for the corresponding cache-effectiveness view.
spec.title: L3 Cache Miss Rate — Per CCX (misses/sec)

spec.query: SELECT non_negative_derivative(mean("value"), 1s) FROM "amd_l3" WHERE ("host" =~ /^$host$/ AND "event" = 'l3_lookup_state.l3_hit') AND $timeFilter GROUP BY time($__interval), "ccx" fill(null)

spec.description:
Rate of L3 cache hits per CCX. Complement to the miss rate — a warm working set shows high hits and low misses. Source: `l3_lookup_state.l3_hit` from `amd_l3`.

Elevated hit rates on a CCX suggest that CCX is doing repeated work on data that fits within its 32 MiB L3 slice — typical of a strategy holding a small hot dataset in memory.

For the effectiveness ratio (hits/(hits+misses)), see the dedicated L3 hit ratio panel. Absolute hit rate here is useful for spotting CCX activity, not efficiency.
spec.title: L3 Cache Hit Rate — Per CCX (hits/sec)

spec.query: SELECT non_negative_derivative(mean("value"), 1s) FROM "amd_core" WHERE ("host" =~ /^$host$/ AND "event" = 'ic_tag_hit_miss.instruction_cache_miss' AND "role" = 'trading') AND $timeFilter GROUP BY time($__interval), "core" fill(null)

spec.description:
Rate of L1 instruction cache misses per trading core. High values indicate the CPU is fetching code from L2/L3/RAM, which stalls the front-end pipeline. Source: `ic_tag_hit_miss.instruction_cache_miss` from `amd_core`.

Normal hot loops stay below 10K/sec. Occasional 100K-1M/sec bursts on cold code paths (initialization, error handling) are fine. Sustained 10x jumps on a previously-quiet core suggest a new code path is running.

Mitigation: reduce hot-path code size, enable huge pages for the text segment (`transparent_hugepage=always`), or use profile-guided optimization to keep hot code together. To trace which code is missing, use `perf record -e ic_tag_hit_miss.instruction_cache_miss -C <core>`.
spec.title: I-Cache Miss Rate — Per Trading Core (misses/sec)

spec.query: SELECT non_negative_derivative(mean("value"), 1s) FROM "amd_core" WHERE ("host" =~ /^$host$/ AND "event" = 'ls_l1_d_tlb_miss.all' AND "role" = 'trading') AND $timeFilter GROUP BY time($__interval), "core" fill(null)

spec.description:
Rate of L1 data TLB misses per trading core. Every miss causes a page-table walk (~50 cycles). High rates mean the workload accesses more virtual pages than the TLB can cache (Zen 5 dTLB = 96 entries). Source: `ls_l1_d_tlb_miss.all` from `amd_core`.

Normal HFT code stays below 100K/sec because working sets are small. Sustained rates above 1M/sec across many cores indicate a memory-scattering access pattern.

Mitigation: enable transparent huge pages (`madvise` or `always` mode) or use `MAP_HUGETLB` for large allocations. Huge pages give 2 MiB TLB coverage per entry vs 4 KiB, so working set the TLB can cover grows from ~400 KiB to ~200 MiB.
spec.title: dTLB Miss Rate — Per Trading Core (misses/sec)

spec.query: SELECT non_negative_derivative(mean("value"), 1s) FROM "amd_core" WHERE ("host" =~ /^$host$/ AND "event" = 'ex_ret_brn_misp' AND "role" = 'trading') AND $timeFilter GROUP BY time($__interval), "core" fill(null)

spec.description:
Rate of retired mispredicted branches per trading core. Each mispredict costs ~15-20 cycles (pipeline flush and refetch). Source: `ex_ret_brn_misp` from `amd_core`.

Absolute rate correlates with branch density in the code — hot loops with lots of branches naturally see high rates. What matters is the trend, not the level. Sudden increases on a previously-clean core suggest a new code path with data-dependent branching.

Mitigation: profile-guided optimization, `__builtin_expect` hints, or branchless code (SIMD select, conditional moves). To find which branches misspredict, use `perf record -e ex_ret_brn_misp -C <core>` and check `perf report`.
spec.title: Branch Mispredictions — Per Trading Core (misp/sec)

spec.query: SELECT non_negative_derivative(mean("value"), 1s) FROM "amd_core" WHERE ("host" =~ /^$host$/ AND "event" = 'ex_ret_ops' AND "role" = 'trading') AND $timeFilter GROUP BY time($__interval), "core" fill(null)

spec.description:
Rate of retired micro-ops per trading core. Zen splits x86 instructions into micro-ops for execution. The ratio `ex_ret_ops / ex_ret_instr` reveals macro-op fusion — typically 1.2-1.5x on Zen 5. Source: `ex_ret_ops` from `amd_core`.

µOp rate is a truer throughput measure than instruction rate for cross-workload comparison, because it accounts for how many micro-ops each x86 instruction decomposes into.

Divergence between µOp rate and instruction rate on the same core is expected — SIMD instructions decompose into more µOps than plain scalar ops. Sudden ratio changes may indicate code path shifts.
spec.title: Retired µOps Rate — Per Trading Core (ops/sec)

spec.query: SELECT mean("value") FROM "amd_uncore" WHERE ("host" =~ /^$host$/ AND "metric" = 'Total_Mem_Bw_GB_s') AND $timeFilter GROUP BY time($__interval), "scope" fill(previous)

spec.description:
Total memory read + write bandwidth in GB/s. `system` = sum of both sockets; `package-0` and `package-1` are per-socket totals. Source: AMDuProfPcm `Total_Mem_Bw` (GB/s) from `amd_uncore`.

HFT trading hosts typically stay under 10 GB/s system-wide with small working sets. Elevated values (>30 GB/s) indicate memory-streaming workloads and increase latency.

Step-shape lines reflect the 5-min sampling cadence — µProf captures for 30 seconds, then holds until the next cycle. Asymmetry between package-0 and package-1 indicates strategies pinned to one socket. Verify with `numactl --hardware` and `numactl --show <pid>`.
spec.title: Memory Bandwidth — System + Per Socket (GB/s)
